summary:
Hermes Finder is a browser extension for Firefox, Chrome and Opera. It helps everyday readers check climate claims while they read an article. News articles often cite scientific papers as their sources, but most people will never read them. Hermes Finder shows the actual data instead, quickly and clearly.

The extension finds climate claims in the article on its own and underlines them. It works in many languages, including English, Polish and German. You can also select any sentence, right-click it and choose "Analyze with Hermes Finder". Clicking a claim opens a panel in the corner of the page with charts. Each chart puts data from several institutions side by side, including NASA, NOAA, Copernicus, the Met Office, JMA and Berkeley Earth, so the results can be compared reliably.

Hovering over a chart shows the exact value for any year, with the name of the institution. Clicking a name in the legend hides that series. Any chart can be enlarged, and the "More" button opens the full analysis in a new tab. The data covers temperature, rainfall, sea level, sea ice, CO₂ and methane, emissions, renewable energy, and even Mars and the other planets.

AI only picks which datasets to show. It never makes up numbers and never says whether a claim is true: the conclusion is up to the reader. The article text stays in the browser. Only the clicked claim and the page title are sent to the server.
details:
Hermes Finder is a browser extension for Firefox, Chrome and Opera that checks climate claims inside the news article you are reading. As you read, it finds sentences that make checkable claims about the climate, such as "winters in Poland are getting warmer" or "sea level is rising faster and faster", and underlines them. You can also select any sentence and right-click "Analyze with Hermes Finder". Clicking a claim opens a small panel in the corner of the page with charts of real measurements. Each chart puts data from several institutions side by side: NASA, NOAA, Copernicus/ECMWF, the Met Office, JMA, Berkeley Earth and others. Hovering over a chart shows the exact value for any year and which institution measured it. You can hide sources in the legend, enlarge a chart, or open the full analysis in a new tab.

Behind the panel is our own server. A language model (Google Gemini) reads the claim and picks which datasets, regions and years are relevant. The server then downloads the data directly from the institutions. It converts the data to common units and baselines, computes trends and differences between sources, and draws the charts. If the language model is unavailable, a rule-based planner picks the datasets instead.

Benefits and intended impact

News articles about climate often cite scientific papers as their sources, and most readers will never open them. The raw data exists, but it is spread across dozens of websites in different formats, units and baselines. Hermes Finder turns that into a chart in a few seconds, without leaving the article. Because we compare many datasets at once, readers can see whether institutions agree, not just trust a single number. We want ordinary people to check claims before believing or sharing them, and teachers, students and journalists to get source data quickly.

Tools and technologies

- Backend: Python with FastAPI, Uvicorn, httpx, NumPy, SciPy and Pydantic.

- AI: Google Gemini, used only to pick datasets.

- Extension: JavaScript on Manifest V3, with charts drawn as SVG by our own code.

- Web app: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Chart.js.

- Data: about 60 datasets, including NASA, NOAA, Copernicus/ECMWF, the Met Office, JMA, Berkeley Earth, Open-Meteo, Our World in Data, Eurostat, PSMSL, SILSO and the Mars Climate Database.

- Testing: automated tests in Firefox and Chromium, and an evaluation set of test claims for the planner.

What makes it creative

Most AI tools answer in text and can make up numbers. We flipped that: the AI is a librarian, not an expert. It decides which data to open but never writes a number and never gives a verdict. Every value comes straight from the source, and the conclusion is the reader's. The tool also works inside the article, at the moment the reader meets the claim, instead of sending them somewhere else. It even covers Mars and the other planets.

Factors we considered

- Trust: no invented numbers, a clear source for every value, and no "true/false" verdicts that could seem politically biased.

- Privacy: the article text stays in the browser. Only the clicked claim and the page title are sent to the server.

- Accessibility: a 13-language interface chosen by the user's country, keyboard navigation, and colorblind-safe chart colors.

- Reliability: the tool still works without the AI, and data is cached so later answers are fast.

- Fair comparison: datasets measured against different baselines are converted to a common reference before they are compared.
